div.p: This paper describes a simulation framework called DRTSS, which allows its users to easily construct discreteevent simulators of complex, multi-paradigm, distributed real-time systems. Preliminary, high-level system designs can be entered into DRTSS to gain initial insight into the timing feasibility of the system. Later, detailed hierarchical designs can be evaluated and more detailed analysis can be undertuken. DRTSS is a member of the PERTS family of timing-oriented prototyping and verification tools [I 71. It complements the PERTS schedulability analyzer tool by dealing with complex real-time systems for which a priori schedulability analysis is diflcult or impossible.

div.head: Introduction
div.p: This paper describes a simulation framework called DRTSS, which allows its users to easily construct discreteevent simulators of complex, multi-paradigm, distributed real-time systems. By using DRTSS, designers or analysts (called simulationists' hereafter) of complex real-time systems can easily enter a system design, including timing parameters, and run experiments to determine whether the system has the desired timing properties.

DRTSS is a member of the PERTS (Prototyping Environment for Real-Time Systems) family of timing-oriented prototyping and verification tools [ 171. In addition to DRTSS, PERTS provides a schedulability analysis tool for systems that yield to deterministic mathematical analysis. However, several aspects of complex real-time systems make an a priori schedulability analysis difficult or impossible. For example, active resources in the system may be scheduled using different scheduling algorithms, communication times may be nondeterministic, and so forth.

'Following standard usage in the simulation literature In order to determine the timing properties of such systems, we tum to simulation methods. While simulation methods have been extensively used, most simulators are designed around a single scheduling paradigm and do not focus on real-time issues. They are therefore not readily applicable to complex real-time systems. DRTSS fills this gap. It provides a suite of modern task assignment, task scheduling, and resource-access control algorithms. Simulationists can select from the existing algorithms and construct simulators of systems that use multiple algorithms. It also allows simulationists to write code for new algorithms and insert them into DRTSS for later use.

DRTSS has three major components. The parameters for a particular simulation run are supplied by the search controller, which can use a variety of search strategies to find extremes in the timing behavior of the simulated system. The main component is the core execution engine, which executes a discrete-event simulation run with a given set of simulation parameters. As events are generated by the execution engine, they are analyzed by the third component, called SETZ (the system for extraction of timing information).

DRTSS differs from most other simulation frameworks in that it does not take the traditional queueing theoretical view. Instead, the execution engine is based on a flexible model of simulated computation called the live task model. In this model, each task represents a unit of work that is done in the simulated system, and tasks have executable code that defines their behavior. The simulator provides a virtual-time execution environment for the tasks. Though many types of tasks can be implemented within DRTSS, we provide built-in support for the standard PERTS model of real-time systems. This model is based on tusk graphs and resource graphs.

Following this introduction, Section 2 summarizes related work. Section 3 discusses the design objectives of DRTSS. Section 4 briefly describes the real-time systems model used by DRTSS. Section 5 provides an overview of the DRTSS framework. Sections 6,7, and 8 give more detail about the search controller, the execution engine, and SETI, respectively. Section 9 discusses current implementation status and future work, and concludes the paper.

div.head: Related Work
div.p: Simulation environment suppliers who want to provide maximum generality have created simulation languages [ 16, 51 rather than higher-level tools such as DRTSS. The trade-off for generality is that the simulationist must program the simulator from scratch, although the special features of simulation languages make this task easier than it might be with a general-purpose language. Traditional simulation languages trace their heritage directly back to the 1960's. Traditional simulation languages [16] still in use are GPSS/H, GPSS World, SIMSCRIPT 11.5, SIMAN V, and SLAMSYSTEM. Simula [32], though no longer in common use, introduced many of the object-oriented ideas used in modem languages. More modem though somewhat less widely used languages include HSL [22], SIMDL [ 111, and SIL [14]. CSIM [23] is an example of a simulation "language" which is not a language in the true sense but a function library for a general-purpose language.

Network simulators such as NetSim, BONeS, and the framework in [21] are similar in objectives and style to DRTSS but target general networked systems rather than real-time systems. These simulators typically only simulate network activity; they do not provide a way to simulate task execution on processors under a variety of scheduling algorithms.

Among the simulation systems targeted towards realtime systems is Stoyenko's "schedanalyzer" [28], a task run-length analyzer. The schedanalyzer allows its users to determine the execution time of programs written in the Real-Time Euclid language and executed in the Real-Time Euclid run-time system. Scheduler 1-2-3 [30], part of the ARTS project [3 11, provides schedulability anlysis and synthetic workload generation but is aimed at a specific hardware environment.
The work most closely related to DRTSS is STRESS

Unlike DRTSS, STRESS defines its own language, which is used for describing both the system to be modelled and how to execute the system. STRESS is therefore in the language category of simulation tools. Another difference is that STRESS focuses exclusively on hard real-time systems while DRTSS is designed for both hard and soft real-time systems. This leads to the inclusion of different capabilities. For example, DRTSS allows for task migration and global scheduling algorithms such as load balancers, while in STRESS tasks are allocated statically and scheduled locally. Other differences exist also. For instance, STRESS has no analog to the DRTSS input variable/search controller/run length control system.

div.head: Goals
div.p: The overall goal for DRTSS is to allow the simulationist to model the widest possible variety of real-time systems in a natural manner and at the desired level of detail. We have designed DRTSS so it supports the simulation of complex distributed real-time systems with many different active resources such as CPUs, networks, sensors, storage units, graphical displays, and so forth. These resources are often scheduled according to fundamentally different algorithms. Therefore, DRTSS must be able to support many different scheduling paradigms, minimally including the following:
traditional uniprocessor and multiprocessor scheduling algorithms for general task sets;
scheduling algorithms for periodic tasks, with servers for aperiodic tasks;
end-to-end scheduling algorithms;
imprecise computation scheduling algorithms for quality-of-service tradeoffs; and arbitrary user-defined scheduling algorithms
In particular, DRTSS is designed to be useful as a tool for exploring the interaction between scheduling algorithms on the various resources and at different levels of the scheduling hierarchy.

With DRTSS, the simulationist can account for the overhead of scheduling algorithms and the effects of their implementations in a realistic way. A factor in scheduling overhead is the time and resources used to carry out scheduling activities. The simulationist is able to simulate the strategy used by a scheduler to schedule time for its own scheduling activities.

DRTSS does not require the simulationist to do any (traditional) programming in order to configure and instantiate a basic simulator. As stated earlier, simulationists may, at their option, implement their own scheduling algorithms.

Tasks that have been implemented (i.e. those tasks for which the simulationist supplies executable code) can be executed during DRTSS simulation runs. Thus DRTSS allows emulation of parts of the software system.

div.head: Real-Time Systems Model
div.p: While the DRTSS execution engine is flexible enough to support alternate models, our primary model of real-time systems is the standard PERTS taskhesource graph model. Special support for this model is built into DRTSS. A PERTS resource graph is used to describe the underlying hardware platform and system software, while a PERTS task graph is used to describe the application software running on the platform in terms of the work it does. (A complete description of these models can be found in [26].)

Each vertex in a resource graph represents either an active or passive resource. The defining characteristic of an active resource, called aprocessor from here on, is that it can cause a task to make progress. A processor is usually referred to as a server in queueing models. Examples of processors are CPUs, disk drives, and network transmission lines. On the other hand, a passive resource alone can never cause a task to make progress. Examples of passive resources are database locks and memory. Many resources can be modelled either as active or passive depending on the point of view of the simulationist; for instance, disk drives and network transmission lines may be modelled either way in many cases. We further classify a passive resource as either a physical (hardware) or logical (software) resource. The parameters of a resource vertex specify information such as the number of units of the resource represented by the vertex, as well as rules governing the usage of the resource.

Both processors and passive resources may have associated scheduling algorithms. Scheduling algorithms for passive resources are usually referred to as resource-access control protocols and are provided as extensions of processor scheduling algorithms.

The edges in the resource graph are of two types. A containment edge is directed and indicates an is-a-component-of relationship, directly supporting object-based decomposition. The subgraph containing only these edges is a forest of component trees. With respect to a component tree, the parent of a physical resource is fixed, but the parent of a logical resource may change at run time. In other words, a logical resource may migrate.

An accessibility edge, on the other hand, is undirected. At least one of the vertices adjacent to an accessibility edge represents a processor. A task running on a processor represented by the processor vertex adjacent to an accessibility edge can (remotely) access any passive resource represented by a vertex in the component tree rooted at the vertex at the other end of the edge.

The task graph is directed and acyclic. Each vertex represents a task to be executed on some processor. Edges in the task graph represent dependency relationships between tasks. There may be more than one connected component in the graph. Tasks may be periodic, aperiodic with muitiple executions, or single-execution. If a task executes multiple times, and if the distinction is important, we refer to each execution as a tusk instance or simply instance. Information about time and resource requirements and timing constraints of individual tasks are provided by the parameters of vertices representing them. The parameters of the edge between two verticies give us information about the dependency between the corresponding tasks and the amount of data exchanged between the tasks.

div.head: DRTSS Simulation Framework
div.p: Again, the DRTSS simulation framework has three major components. The search controller chooses parameters for a particular simulation run and supplies them to the execution engine, which does the simulation run. As events are generated by the execution engine, they are analyzed by SETI.

The execution engine takes the process-oriented world view, widely regarded as the orientation of choice [5] in the simulation literature. By saying that the execution engine is process-oriented, as opposed to event-oriented or activityoriented, we mean that event handling and generation code is organized as processes (i.e. "task instances" in our real-time systems terminology), not events or activities.

From a program design point of view, the DRTSS execution engine is object-oriented. This is not at all inconsistent with the process-oriented world view. As argued in [7], we can derive the greatest benefit from an object-oriented simulator design when we take a process-oriented worldview. In fact, many modem simulation systems have both a process-oriented world view and an object-oriented design.

The execution engine is comprised of several major objects. The driver controls the overall operation of the engine. Eachprocessor has an associated microkernal that interfaces it to the rest of the simulator. Each processor may have one or more scheduling algorithms that control the allocation of the processor and optionally some passive resources to task instances. Task instances are generated from tasks, which act as templates. Anprimitive event (or simply event) marks the occurrence of a scheduling-related activity, such as instance creation, instance completion, or resource allocation.

The execution engine generates many events over the course of a simulation run, and during a single simulation experiment the search controller may start many simulation runs. Therefore, a large number of events are generated. In most cases the simulationist is not interested in the events themselves, but rather in less voluminous, higher level information. To generate higher level information in DRTSS, the simulationist specifies a compound event, which is a boolean expression built up out of (primitive) events. SETI watches for compound events in conceptually the same way that a logic analyzer watches for its trigger conditions. However, the events may be parameterized, so SETI needs to do unification (in the sense of logic languages) of event parameters.

The DRTSS framework has been implemented by a tool called SimBuilder which employs a graphical user interface. Technically, the DRTSS simulation framework is separate from the SimBuilder tool that implements it, which is in turn separate from the DRTSS simulator that the simulationist generates by using the tool. Where there is no ambiguity, we will hereafter refer to the DRTSS framework, the DRTSS SimBuilder tool, and a DRTSS simulator simply as DRTSS.

div.head: Search Controller
div.p: The search controller is a subsystem that directs the simulator's search through the search parameter space. Search parameters in DRTSS are any numeric parameters of tasks (e.g. ready time, execution time, deadline), processors (e.g. processing rate, context switch time), or resources (e.g. acquisition time, deaquisition time) that are marked as search Parameters by the simulationist. The simulationist specifies upper and lower bounds and the granularity of the search. A given search controller may also allow the simulationist to provide hints to help the controller in its search. For example, in the simple linear search controller supplied with the SimBuilder, the simulationist can specify the direction of the search (lower bound to upper bound or vice versa), the nesting of the search (which search parameter is varied the fastest, which is varied the next fastest, etc.), and a condition under which the search is to stop (typically when no deadlines are missed).

A search parameter normally corresponds directly to a task, processor, or resource parameter. However, if the task, processor, or resource parameter is a random variable, the search parameter may be a parameter of the random variable. For example, if the execution time of a task is given as an exponentially distributed random variable, then the mean of the distribution may be a search parameter.

In the last step of configuring a simulation experiment (just before the simulator starts to run) the search controller is given a reference (in the programming sense) to a set of search parameter objects. Each search parameter maintains its own upper and lower bounds, its granularity, and its current value. The tuple of current values of all search parameters defines a point in the search space. Whenever a batch of simulation runs is about to begin, the search controller is given the opportunity to pick a new point in the search space, which it does by modifying the current values of one or more search parameter objects.

It is a simple matter to add a new search algorithm to the SimBuilder. The programmer-simulationist2 simply derives a new class from the provided search controller abstract base class and adds a few lines of code so that the new search controller shows up as an option in the graphical user interface.
*We use this term to distinguish a simulationist who is not only an enduser of the SimBuilder, but who wishes to extend it via C++ programming

div.head: Design Search
div.p: Depending on its purpose, a search though the parameter space of the simulated system can be classified as either a design search or a validation search. The distinction is important because different search controllers and data visualization methods are required for each. We discuss design search first.

In a design search there are two classes of input parameters. Some parameters are considered to be fixed; they are part of the specification and the simulationist is not at liberty to change them. The simulationist may, however, be able to choose (or trade-off) values of other parameters, which we call design parameters. The goal of the design search in a hard real-time system is to see for which combinations of values of the design parameters the system will meet some criterion (usually the criterion is no deadlines missed). In a soft real-time system, the goal is to minimize a value associated with the criterion, which is often referred to as the objective function. We consider the former case first, using the example of deadlines missed to make the discussion more concrete.
In the case of PERTS taskhesource graph input we have the following potential search parameters:

div.head: For tasks
div.p: For resources Deadline ProcessingRate DeacquisitionTime DropDeadline

div.head: Period
div.p: The semantics of this particular set of parameters indicates that it will not be difficult to find a combination of values for all deadlines are met. The reason for this is that all of the parameters except ReleaseTime and DropDeadline have the clear semantics that larger values (or smaller values as the case may be) will make it easier for the system to meet deadline^.^ Scheduling anomalies notwithstanding, in any practical system it is highly unlikely that many combinations of parameters (with values near the "easy" end of the range) will need to be tried in order to find a combination where deadlines are met. In contrast, in validation search we must treat scheduling anomalies seriously, as we will discuss shortly.

Ideally, rather than finding one set of parameters for which the system meets deadlines, we should find the shape of the boundary between the regions of the design parameter space that yield "good" and "bad" systems. Once the 3This is not necessarily true for systems where it is possible for some subset of tasks to be running other than the m highest-priority ready-to-run tasks (assuming an m-processor system), because scheduling anomalies are possible. boundary is known, the simulationist can then choose a set of parameter values from the good region that achieves the desired tradeoffs. Since an N-dimensional search space has an ( N -1)-dimensional boundary, this technique is only effective for N less than or equal to about 5. Much beyond 5, it becomes impractical to exhaustively simulate all the points in the search space to find the boundary.
The problem of finding the values of design parameters that minimize some objective function is quite different.

Here, if we can indeed find a combination of parameter values where the objective function takes on its minimum possible value, then the search is successful. We can either terminate the search or try to find another combination that achieves the minimum possible value, in order to give the system designer an alternative set of parameter values from which to choose. (By minimum possible value we mean the minimum value that the function could take on for any values of the design parameters. For example, the minimum possible value of the completion time of a task is equal to its execution time,) If we cannot find a combination that gives us the minimum possible value, we hope to find a combination that yields the actual minimum value of the function for the given ranges of design parameters. Either way, we need a global-minimum search algorithm capable of dealing with high-dimensional spaces. Simulated annealing [ 151, genetic algorithms [ 131, and combinations thereof [ 1, 33,291 are commonly used for such problems.

div.head: Validation Search
div.p: In a validation search, some of the input parameters will be constants, and others will be random variables in order to accurately reflect their true values in the system being modelled. For example, the period of a task may be a constant value but the execution time of the task may be evenly distributed in a range of possible values. The goal of the validation search is to determine whether the system will always meet its deadlines, regardless of the actual values that the random parameters take on as the system executes. Stated another way, we wish to determine whether the system can meet all its deadlines under worst-case conditions. We cannot assume that the schedule that occurs when all parameters take on their worst-case values is the worst-case schedule. As we mentioned before, scheduling anomalies can occur. In this case the anomalies cannot be dismissed, since we are looking for the worst case, not just one acceptable case.

To do a validation search we change the nondeterministic input parameters into search parameters, and then search for schedules in which the completion times of instances of each task are maximized. The search methods given below depend on deterministic simulations for their validity, so no parameters may be left nondeterministic. It is problematic to restate a nondeterministic input parameter as a search parameter if its distribution has a "long tail", that is, if there is a nontrivial probability that it takes on a very wide range of values. The alternatives are to cut off the tail at some point or to increase the granularity of the search. In the former case we do not have complete coverage while the latter covers the entire tail but leaves larger holes between the (discrete) values chosen. A sophisticated validation-oriented search controller would allow the search parameters to be specified in terms of their distributions, rather than requiring by-hand conversion to deterministic search parameters. In this case the search controller can dynamically adjust the granularity of the search over a range of values in proportion to the probability of those values occurring, so that there is denser coverage of higher probability values and sparser coverage of lower probability values.

We are developing a schedulabilityanalysis-driven search methodology as one way to attack validation search. Whenever possible, we use analysis methods from [ 121 as bounding tools to prune the search tree. The real-time systems models used in [ 121 are special cases of the PERTS taskhesource graph model. In order to use the algorithms from [ 121 in a search controller we must restrict ourselves to these models.

div.head: Execution Engine
div.p: We distinguish between a representation model of a realtime system and the execution model through which we simulate it. By representationmodel we mean a model in the usual sense -thus the PERTS taskhesource graph model is a representation model of real-time systems. A representation model is concerned primarily with describing the structure of the system at some level -it focuses on the problem domain. An execution model, in contrast, is a way of describing how to execute a simulationgiven an instance of a representation model -it focuses on the solutiondomain.

We use the PERTS taskhesource graph model as our primary representation model. The PERTS model is, however, largely without execution semantics so we developed a distinct execution model, which we call the live task model. This model offers a clean way to execute the PERTS taskhesource graph model. Here, by executing a model we mean running a simulation that has input data which is of the form prescribed by the model. The live task model is general enough to execute other representation models of real-time systems, such as trace-driven models.

div.head: Live Task Model
div.p: The live task model uses the same definitions of task, processor and resource as the PERTS representation model. In a traditional computer system simulator, a task does not have executable code associated with it; it is merely a static collection of parameter data. To simulate the execution of instances of such a task, a "work done" counter is incremented when the instance is given simulated execution time, and the simulation engine checks whether the instance should take any "action" at that point in simulated time. The actions are both built into and invoked under the direct control of the execution engine. The processor plays virtually no role in the entire execution process, except as an inactive repository for parameters such as processing rate and data such as a list of tasks running on the processor.

The live task model represents an altemate way to execute the PERTS model (and other models). The live task model draws inspiration from the Actor model [2]. Tasks and scheduling algorithms are essentially a special case of actors; they are stand-alone objects with their own threads of control. Specifically, each task has an associated executable function which is invoked as a separate thread (i.e. lightweight process) when a task instance is created. The function does not retum until the instance finishes executing, so the lifetime of the thread matches the lifetime of the task instance object. The purpose of the function is to simulate what the task is supposed to be doing in the modelled system, at least from the timing point of view (but not necessarily limited to the timing point of view). A canonical task function is shown in C-style pseudocode below; hereafter we will refer to any such task function as Execute ( ) .
void Execute() { while (there-is-another-action-to-do) I Compute(execution-time_until_action); Do-action(action);

div.head: Compute(remaining-execution-time); 3
div.p: When a task instance needs to do some (simulated) work, it calls the Compute ( ) function (which is supplied by the execution engine),passing the amount of time that it needs to execute. The Compute ( ) functiondoesnot returnuntilthe instance has been given its requested execution time. After Compute ( ) returns, Execute ( ) will typically take some action; in the case of PERTS tasks this will be either to lock or unlock a resource.
From the point of view of the DRTSS framework, the Execute ( ) function can be implemented in a number of ways:
1. A single Execute ( ) function operates on static task data. This function is hard-wired into the execution engine. This is sufficient for PERTS task graph tasks.
Several different Execute ( ) functions are hardwired into the execution engine. This would support different "types" of tasks.
Different Execute ( ) functions are compiled separately from the execution engine and bound at link time, or even at run time.

A single Execute ( ) function that isan interpreter for a task description language is written. This differsonly in degree, not in kind from (l), since an Execute ( ) function that follows instructions supplied in its input task data is essentially a simple interpreter. Nonetheless, a "real" interpreter could be a full programming language with conditional constructs, loops, etc. Tasks in the STRESS language [3] are effectively in this category.
The approach taken in SimBuilder is option 2.

Processors play an active role in the live task model. A processor has a short run queue of task instances that are ready to run. It is the responsibility of some scheduling algorithm (normally "the" scheduling algorithm of that processor) to keep the run queue non-empty. When directed by the execution engine to run for a certain length of time, the processor simply takes the task instance at the head of the run queue and allows it to "execute" for the specified amount of simulated time. If this brings the executed time up to the amount requested by the task's Compute ( ) , then Compute ( ) is allowed to retum. The task's Execute ( ) routine proceeds to its next action or next Compute ( ) as the case may be.

div.head: Benefits of the Live Task Model
div.p: The fundamental difference between the live task execution model and traditional execution models is that in the former, tasks directly take their own actions, while in the latter the execution engine invokes actions on behalf of the tasks. This seemingly small difference has important ramifications in an extensible execution engine framework. In the live task model tasks are objects not only from the object-oriented programming point of view, but also from the object-oriented design point of view. This is a much stronger statement, as argued in [9, pages 201-2071. The behavior of tasks is encapsulated within the task object. Consequently, the programmer-simulationist needs to know very little about the internals of the execution engine.

The execution time of a task need not be a constant nor a random variable taken from a single distribution. It can be made a function of time or of some state of the system, since the programmer-simulationist can program the Execute ( ) function with whatever behavior he wishes. For example, the execution time of a task that manipulates a priority queue of items may change as the size of the queue increases.

Since tasks can execute real code in the live task model, it becomes possible to implement scheduling algorithms as tasks, instead of hard-wiring them into the execution engine as is normally done. A model with scheduling algorithms as tasks allows for more accurate modeling of scheduling overhead. Traditionally in real-time systems analysis, we assume either that scheduling overhead is negligible or that it can be accounted for by adding a constant to the execution time of the tasks. For purposes of deriving worst-case schedulability bounds, adding a constant worst-case factor may be appropriate (in fact it may be a necessity), but for simulation this approach is usually overly pessimistic. With scheduling algorithms as tasks, the fidelity of accounting for scheduling overhead is raised to the same level as accounting for the execution time of tasks.

Scheduling algorithms have the opportunity to consider their own execution time when making scheduling decisions. That is, a scheduling algorithm may want to schedule time for itself to make further scheduling decisions. Simple priority-driven scheduling algorithms do not need this type of self-awareness, but there are many examples of scheduling algorithms whose time complexity is high enough that scheduling overhead needs to be explicitly treated (recent examples include the Spring Kernel [19] and the optimal algorithm of [ lo]).

The internal structure of the execution engine is cleaner with the task-behavior and scheduler code encapsulated in task objects. Scheduling algorithms benefit from encapsulation as task objects even more so than ordinary tasks, since scheduling algorithms are generally much more complex and their organization has a larger impact on the design of the execution engine. The benefit is partly due to the encapsulation itself, but also due to the fact that this organization parallels the organization of the simulated operating system and the interaction between objects parallels the behavior of objects in the operating system. In other words, the execution engine follows the isomorphic structure principle 19, pages 201-2071. Isomorphic structure with operating systems gives us a measure of confidence in the extensibility of DRTSS and is a great boon to the simulationist who needs to extend the SimBuilder by adding a new scheduling algorithm. It is not necessary to do a paradigm shift to fit the algorithm into the SimBuilder because the algorithm fits into the SimBuilder in the same manner that it would fit into a operating system.

The live task model allows programmer-simulationists to use DRTSS for more than simulation in the strict sense. As argued in 1341 and [21], in many cases of designing and building systems, it is beneficial to tie the modelling and simulation effort more directly to the design and development process. One way of accomplishing this is to allow simulationists to start with pure simulation of their systems and progress toward emulation without changing environments. This extends the simulationactivity in aproject much deeper into the development cycle. It allows the system to be built incrementally, without having to totally switch gears from "simulation mode" to "development mode". For example, implementing and evaluating a proposed scheduling algorithm may be a substantial part of the simulation effort in a real-time system design. If the simulation is done using a simulation language such a SIMSCRIPT, then when development begins the scheduling algorithm will have to be re-implemented (and equally importantly re-tested) in the target language, which is likely to be C, C++ or Ada. In contrast, by using NEST [34] (which is oriented towards networking systems development) or DRTSS, the simulationist can implement the scheduling algorithm in any language that can be linked with C++ (or with some additional effort, in any target language that runs on Unix).

An additional benefit of allowing live tasks is that the simulationist can easily implement a hybrid model as conceived in [8] or [24] and formally classified by Sargent [25]. A hybrid model allows the simulationist to take advantage of both analytic and simulation methods. The simulationist may have a good analytic model for certain subsystems of a large system, but cannot model the system as a whole analytically. Simulation of the subsystems together with the entire system would be too costly in terms of simulation running time. In this case the simulationist can create a hybrid model by using DRTSS for the system-level simulation whileusing the analytic model to compute the running times of tasks on the appropriate subsystems on the fly.

div.head: System for Extraction of Timing Information
div.p: The output of the DRTSS execution engine is a set of primitive events, such as "task-preempted" and "tas k-aborted," partially ordered according to the instants of their occurrences. A primitive event is a marker of a particular scheduling-related activityit occupies only a time instant, rather than an interval. Primitive events are parameterized as necessary to give complete information regarding what activity occurred. For example a task-preempted event is parameterized by the preempted task name, the preempted task instance number, the preempting task name, the preempting task instance number, and the processor on which the preemption took place.

The set of primitive events can be viewed directly. However, in most cases we neither require nor desire large volumes of low-level event information. Usually we are interested in counts of the occurrences or probability distributions of the intervals between occurrences. We are also interested in detecting particular patterns of primitive events that have particular temporal relationships, which we call compound events. The SETI subsystem provides these capabilities to DRTSS. The subsystem includes a compound event specification language, called CELL, based on first-order logic [27]. CELL facilitates the recognition of compound events and the extraction of pertinent timing information.

div.head: Output Variables
div.p: The primary objects in SETI are an simulationistspecified collection of output variables. An output vari- able is used to gather statistics on a particular primitive or (more usually) compound event. An output event has a trigger, which is a compound event specified as a CELL expression. A CELL expression is comprised of primitive events, parenthesis (for grouping, as usual), and the operators A N D , O R , = , >, >=, <, <=, <>, and -. The operators are used to express relationships between events.

An output variable also has a data generator expression, which is used to generate a single numerical value whenever the trigger$res. A sequence of these numerical values is called an output stream, and the output variable automatically maintains statistics (mean value, variance, confidence intervals) on its output stream.

The parameters of primitive events may be bound to literal values, or may be unbound variables. For instance, in the previous example the preempted task name parameter may be bound to Flight-control (assuming Flight-control is thenameof ataskinthetaskgraph), while the preempted task instance number is left unbound as a variable named n.

As primitive events are generated by the execution engine, each output variable attempts to match each generated event against all the primitive events in the trigger. If a match occurs, the parameters of the matching primitive event are bound to the values of the parameters of the generated event. This process is similar to unification in Prolog. A givenmatch may cause the entire trigger expression to be satisfied, in which case we say that the trigger$res. This is similar to deduction in Prolog.

As separate parts of the output variable specification, the simulationist supplies the data generator expression in terms of the times that events in the trigger are matched, plus a user event to post. When the trigger fires, two things happen: (1) the data generator is evaluated and the resulting value is written to an output stream, and (2) the user event which tells the rest of the system that the compound event has just "occurred" is posted. Other output variables may have triggers that depend on the user event. Thus higher level compound events can be built out of more primitive ones.

As an example, suppose that we are interested in the average completion time of instances of task Flight-control. An appropriate trigger would be and an appropriate data generator would be finishstart The primitive events ins tance-generated and instance-completed are parameterized by a task name, an instance number, and a processor where the event occurred. In this example, the task name and processor are bound to literal values while the instance number is left as a variable, to be bound by generated events during a simulation run. Suppose that the simulation is run and the event i n s tan ce-genera ted [ F 1 i g h t-con trol , 1, AvionicsComputer] is generated at time 5. This event is matched against each of the event specifications in the trigger.

A match is found with instance-generated [Flight-control, n, AvionicsComputer], and n is therefore bound to 1. Also, start is assigned a value of 5. Later, when instance-completed[Flight-control, 1, AvionicsComputer] occurs at time 11, finish is assigned a value of 11, and the trigger fires. The data generator is evaluated, and the resulting value of 6 is written to the output stream.

div.head: The Event Stream
div.p: The output event stream provides a clean separation between the execution engine and SETI. Data flow in DRTSS is summarized in Figure 1 below. The execution engine generates a stream of events; SETI monitors this stream and detects compound events as described above. It also posts user events back into the event stream if the simulationist so chooses in the configuration of the output variables. If this were all the data flow in the system, it would be natural to simply dump events to a file and implement SETI as a standalone post-simulation analysis package. However, there is an important "back edge" in the data flow diagram. The back edge arises because the output variables play a large part in determining how long a simulation run should continue and how many simulation runs should be made at the current point in the search space. Each output variable maintains its own statistics, and the simulation continues until the confidence interval of each output variable is less than or equal to the value specified by the simulationist. Of course, the output variable has no way of knowing how long this will take a priori; at run time it keeps the execution engine up to date as to whether the specified condition has been satisfied.

MacNair and Welch identify the need for output-variablebased run length control as part of a "higher level output analysis interface" [ 181, and the value of this technique to the simulationist is self-evident. Nonetheless, this feature appears to be rarely provided in simulation environments; even recently developed environments such as Q-Sim [6] and STRESS [3] require manual run-length control.

We plan to provide a library of standard output variables (both CELL and data generator expressions) for the Sim-Builder. These output variables can be added to a given simulation experiment configuration using simple cut-andpaste.

Other analysis tools that operate on either the raw event lists or on output variable data streams can be implemented as standalone programs. Also, the simulationist can optionally save the events in the Pablo Self Defining Data Format [4]. Then analysis, visualization, and auralization tools provided by or compatible with the Pablo Performance Analysis Environment [20] can be used to examine the data.

div.head: Future Work and Conclusion
div.p: As o f this writing, implementation of the basic Sim-Builder tool includes a sample search controller, the execution engine with several real-time scheduling algorithms, and the SET1 subsystem. The SimBuilder is written in C++, runs in the UnixIX Window System environment, and has an OSFiMotif based user interface, as are common to all modules of PERTS. A SPARC binary is available via anonymous ftp from ftp.cs.uiuc.edu in the ipubiperts directory, or though the world-wide-web at http://pertsserver.cs.uiuc.edu/software. Source code is also available after completion of a signed licensing agreement.

In conclusion, we view DRTSS as a critical component of PERTS. The overall goal of PERTS is to help practitioners take advantage of recent advances in scheduling theory in the prototyping, design, or re-design of complex realtime systems. DRTSS helps achieve that goal by providing complementary functionality to the schedulability analysis components of PERTS. It allows a wider variety of systems to be evaluated at a greater level of detail, at the cost of obtaining only probabilistic results in most cases and requiring significantly more CPU time than the PERTS schedulability The major focus of future work for DRTSS is to extend yzer.

the framework so that it will support hierarchical simulation. In a sense DRTSS already supports hierarchical simulation in that it allows hybrid simulation through the live task model. An entire sub-simulator can be written as a DRTSS task. However, this does not leverage the existing simulation framework.
